# Computing with chemical organizations

`organization-computing` · *Matsumaru, Speroni di Fenizio, Centler & Dittrich, 2006-2011*

!!! warning "Archived: pruned"
    This entry is not part of the chemistry catalog (set aside from the catalog). It keeps its specification, generator and tests, and `generate_network` still runs it by id, but listings and the LLM tools leave it out. See the [catalog's archive](index.md#archive).

## Introduction

Computing with chemical organizations is a way of designing and checking
chemical programs, developed by Naoki Matsumaru, Peter Dittrich and colleagues
at the University of Jena between 2005 and 2011. In a chemical program the
answer is not written anywhere; it emerges from many local reactions, and it
is hard to predict what a given list of reactions will do. Their proposal is to
treat the answer as *which kinds of molecules survive*, and to use chemical
organization theory to work out, from the reaction list alone, which sets of
molecules can survive at all.

Chemical organization theory is Dittrich and Speroni di Fenizio's theory of
reaction networks, described in chapter 12 of the book. An **organization** is
a set of molecular species with two properties. It is **closed**: reactions
among its members produce nothing outside the set. And it is
**self-maintaining**: every member that some reaction uses up can be made again
by reactions within the set, so the set as a whole does not run down. The
theory shows that whenever the rate equations of a network settle at a steady
state, the species still present form an organization. Finding the
organizations needs only the reactions, not their rates, so it tells the
programmer what a network *can* end up doing whatever the kinetics.

The idea in one example: a chemical XOR gate. Each Boolean variable gets two
species, one meaning "0" and one meaning "1": `a0` and `a1` for input `a`, and
so on. One reaction per row of the truth table makes the right output species,
for example `a1 + b0 -> c1`, and a "particle meets anti-particle" reaction
`c0 + c1 -> ∅` destroys any variable that holds both values at once. Feed in
`a1` and `b0` steadily, and the only organization left is `{a1, b0, c1}`: the
vessel can only end up holding `c1`, the right answer, whatever the starting
contents. Information is carried by the presence or absence of a species, not
by its amount or by the structure of a molecule.

This is a **design and analysis method**, applied to small hand-made reaction
networks: logic gates, a flip-flop, an oscillator and a distributed graph
algorithm. Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe it in chapter 17 (book §17.3.3), among
distributed algorithms built from chemistry. Its nearest neighbours in the
catalog differ in what carries the information. [Gamma](gamma.md) and the
[CHAM](cham.md) compute by rewriting a multiset of symbols and read the answer
from the molecules left; [analog computation with
concentrations](analog-function-crn.md) (§17.4.3) reads numbers off steady-state
concentrations; [Okamoto's switch](okamoto-switch.md) (§17.4.1) is a flip-flop
built from a bistable concentration switch; the [chemical
disperser](disperser.md) (§17.3.1) is another distributed algorithm written as
reactions, but one whose answer is a set of concentrations. Here only the set of
species present matters. Chemical organization theory itself is not a separate
catalog entry.

## How it works

### Two species per bit

Every Boolean variable `x` is represented by two species, `x0` for "x = 0"
and `x1` for "x = 1". A variable is well defined when exactly one of its two
species is present. Both present is a contradiction; neither present means
"not yet set". Concentrations are allowed to fluctuate: what counts in the long
run is which species are present, so the concentrations are, in the book's
words, "reduced to zeros (species absent) or ones (species present)".

The reactions are of two kinds:

- **logical reactions**, one per row of each gate's truth table: the inputs of
  that row react to give the output of that row;
- **destructive reactions** `x0 + x1 -> ∅`, one per variable, so that the two
  values of a bit annihilate on contact.

Inputs are supplied from outside by **inflow reactions** `∅ -> a1`, a constant
feed of the input species. The papers run the networks with mass-action
kinetics in a well-stirred vessel, but the design and the analysis ignore the
rates.

### A worked example: the default XOR

The default network is the XOR gate of book table 17.3:

```
a0 + b0 -> c0
a0 + b1 -> c1
a1 + b0 -> c1
a1 + b1 -> c0
a0 + a1 -> ∅
b0 + b1 -> ∅
c0 + c1 -> ∅
```

Which sets of these six species are organizations? Take `{a1, b0}`. It is not
closed: `a1 + b0 -> c1` makes `c1`, which is outside the set. Add it:
`{a1, b0, c1}` is closed, but not self-maintaining, because the reaction uses up
`a1` and `b0` and nothing in the set makes them again. Now add the inflows
`∅ -> a1` and `∅ -> b0`. The inflows replace what the gate consumes, so
`{a1, b0, c1}` becomes an organization. Every other set fails. Any set holding
`c0` is not self-maintaining, since `c0` is only made from `a0 + b0` or
`a1 + b1`, not from the inputs being fed, while `c1 + c0 -> ∅` destroys it; the
same goes for `a0` and `b1`. So one organization remains, and it contains the
correct output.

Without the inflows the picture is different. Sets of species that do not react
with one another, such as `{a1, c0}`, are trivially closed and
self-maintaining, and Matsumaru et al. (2007) count 15 organizations for the
seven reactions above. Adding one input leaves three; adding both leaves one.
Chemart's generator does not add the inflows (see *Using it*), so the network it
returns is the "no input specified" gate, with the inputs as a starting state.

### Hasse diagrams: computing as moving between organizations

The organizations of a network, ordered by inclusion, are drawn as a **Hasse
diagram**: each organization is a node, and a line joins two organizations when
one contains the other with none in between. The authors describe a
computation as a *movement* in this diagram. Changing an input (swapping the
inflow `∅ -> b0` for `∅ -> b1`, say) changes the diagram, and the vessel moves
to the organization that now exists; species that no longer belong die out
through the destructive reactions. A design is good when each possible output
has its organization and there are no others to get stuck in.

### The maximal independent set program

The second program in the book solves a graph problem. In an undirected graph,
an **independent set** is a set of vertices no two of which share an edge. It is
**maximal** (a MIS) when no further vertex can be added without breaking that
rule. The book's motivation is choosing cluster heads in a wireless network:
the vertices in the set are masters, each other vertex has a master next to it,
and no two masters are neighbours. A graph usually has several maximal
independent sets; any one of them is an answer.

Each vertex `v` gets two species: `s1_v` for "v is in the set" and `s0_v` for
"v is not". Three kinds of reactions follow from the graph (book eqs. 17.5 to
17.7):

- `s0_v + s1_v -> ∅`: the two states of a vertex annihilate;
- for each vertex, one reaction that consumes an "out" molecule of every
  neighbour and makes that many "in" molecules of the vertex itself: if none of
  my neighbours is in the set, I join it;
- for each edge, `s1_u -> s0_v` in both directions: a vertex in the set pushes
  its neighbours out.

Here is the network Chemart generates for the path of three vertices 1–2–3,
the first example of Matsumaru and Dittrich (2006):

```
s0_1 + s1_1 -> ∅
s0_2 + s1_2 -> ∅
s0_3 + s1_3 -> ∅
s0_2 -> s1_1
s0_1 + s0_3 -> 2 s1_2
s0_2 -> s1_3
s1_2 -> s0_1
s1_1 -> s0_2
s1_3 -> s0_2
s1_2 -> s0_3
```

Vertex 2 has two neighbours, so its "join" reaction takes one `s0_1` and one
`s0_3` and makes two `s1_2`. The end vertices have one neighbour each. Read
the set `{s0_1, s1_2, s0_3}`: vertex 2 is in, and its ends are out. `s1_2`
keeps producing `s0_1` and `s0_3`, and these recombine into `s1_2`; nothing
produces `s1_1`, `s1_3` or `s0_2`, so the set is closed and maintains itself.
It is the answer "010". The set `{s1_1, s0_2, s1_3}`, the answer "101", works
the same way. A graph with `N` vertices and `M` edges gives `2N` species and
`2(N + M)` reactions, and the reactions only link a vertex with its
neighbours, so the program can run as a distributed algorithm, one small
compartment per vertex.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). two species per Boolean variable: x0 for x=0 and x1 for x=1; information is encoded by PRESENCE/ABSENCE, not concentration

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: variable). XOR gate: a0+b0 -&gt; c0 ; a0+b1 -&gt; c1 ; a1+b0 -&gt; c1 ; a1+b1 -&gt; c0, plus annihilation x0 + x1 -&gt; (nothing) for each variable. Maximal independent set: s0_j + s1_j -&gt; ; s0_j + s0_k + ... + s0_l -&gt; n_i s1_i (over the n_i neighbours of v_i) ; s1_j -&gt; s0_i for all (v_j, v_i) in E.

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time); or `ssa` (stochastic simulation (Gillespie): individual reaction events happen at random times).

*How the population is bounded:* none

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("organization-computing", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
organization-computing: 6 species, 7 reactions, status=complete
provides: initial-state, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
a0 + b0 -> c0
a0 + b1 -> c1
a1 + b0 -> c1
a1 + b1 -> c0
a0 + a1 -> ∅
b0 + b1 -> ∅
c0 + c1 -> ∅
```

The default call returns the XOR gate above, with inputs `a = 0`, `b = 1`
placed in the initial state as one molecule each. The four logical reactions
always cover the whole truth table; the inputs `a` and `b` change only
`net.initial_state`:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("organization-computing", a=True, b=False)
net.initial_state      # {'a1': 1, 'b0': 1}
```

`net.extras` is empty. The reactions carry no rates (the *Implementation
decisions* below explain why), so Chemart provides the network's structure,
not a simulation.

**The maximal independent set program.** Set `problem="maximal-independent-set"`
and give the graph as a list of undirected edges in `graph`. The default graph
is the path 0–1–2–3, which has three maximal independent sets:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("organization-computing",
                               problem="maximal-independent-set")
print(net.summary())
```

```
organization-computing: 8 species, 14 reactions, status=complete
provides: stoichiometry, topology
```

This network has no initial state. `s1_3` means "vertex 3 is in the set".

**Finding the organizations.** Chemart does not compute organizations. The
function below does it by brute force for small networks: it tries every set of
species, checks closure, and checks self-maintenance with a linear program
(some flux `v`, every entry at least 1, over the reactions that can run in the
set, must leave no species with a negative net production). The `inflow`
argument adds the reactions `∅ -> s` that the papers use to supply inputs.

```python
from itertools import combinations
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog
import chemart

def organisations(net, inflow=()):
    rules = [(r.reactants, r.products) for r in net.reactions]
    rules += [({}, {s: 1}) for s in inflow]            # inflow  ∅ -> s
    ids = [s.id for s in net.species]
    found = []
    for k in range(len(ids) + 1):
        for A in map(set, combinations(ids, k)):
            active = [(l, r) for l, r in rules if set(l) <= A]
            if any(p not in A for _, r in active for p in r):
                continue                               # not closed
            if active:                                 # self-maintaining?
                S = np.array([[r.get(a, 0) - l.get(a, 0) for l, r in active]
                              for a in sorted(A)])
                lp = linprog(np.zeros(len(active)), A_ub=-S, b_ub=np.zeros(len(A)),
                             bounds=[(1, None)] * len(active))
                if lp.status != 0:
                    continue
            found.append(sorted(A))
    return found

xor = chemart.generate_network("organization-computing")
len(organisations(xor))                         # 15
organisations(xor, inflow=["a1"])               # [['a1'], ['a1', 'c0'], ['a1', 'c1']]
organisations(xor, inflow=["a1", "b0"])         # [['a1', 'b0', 'c1']]
```

With all four input pairs the only organization is the correct row of the truth
table: `{a0, b0, c0}`, `{a0, b1, c1}`, `{a1, b0, c1}` and `{a1, b1, c0}`. For the
default MIS graph it finds 9 organizations; the three largest are exactly the
three maximal independent sets, `{1, 3}`, `{0, 3}` and `{0, 2}`:

```
[['s0_0', 's0_2', 's1_1', 's1_3'], ['s0_1', 's0_2', 's1_0', 's1_3'], ['s0_1', 's0_3', 's1_0', 's1_2']]
```

The search doubles with every species, so it is practical up to about a dozen
species: the 12-species network of the six-vertex example under *Results* takes
about four seconds.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `problem` | `enum` | `xor` | structural | which chemical program of the book to generate <br>one of `xor`, `maximal-independent-set` |
| `a` | `bool` | `False` | population | XOR input a; its species a0 or a1 is put in the initial state |
| `b` | `bool` | `True` | population | XOR input b; its species b0 or b1 is put in the initial state |
| `graph` | `list` | `[[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 3]]` | structural | undirected edges [u, v] of the maximal-independent-set instance |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "2 decisions"

    - No rates: the book's analysis is organisational (which species survive), not kinetic.
    - The book gives no MIS instance; the default graph is a 4-vertex path. Edges are undirected, so eq. 17.7 applies in both directions. Inputs a and b only affect the XOR program.

## Results

### Logic gates and circuits

Matsumaru, Centler, Speroni di Fenizio and Dittrich (2007) set out a recipe for
turning any logic circuit into reactions, the one described above, and used
organization theory to check the result. For the XOR gate they count **28
organizations** when the network has only the four logical reactions, **15**
once the three destructive reactions are added, **3** for each single input,
and **one** for each of the four input pairs, always the one containing the
correct output. Because only one organization remains, no other set of species
can be sustained "no matter how we chose the dynamics", regardless of the
initial state. They confirmed this with stochastic simulations (in the MGS and
Copasi simulators) at rate constants 1 for inflows, 0.1 for destruction and
0.001 for the logical reactions, switching the inputs every 100 s: after each
switch the old output decays and the new one appears.

Chemart generates this XOR network, and the organization search above
reproduces all four counts, 28, 15, 3 and 1, on it. The test
`test_xor_gate_follows_truth_table` in `tests/chemistries/test_w1_structure.py`
checks the four logical reactions, the annihilation `c0 + c1 -> ∅` and the
initial state; the organization counts are not part of Chemart's tests, and
Chemart cannot rerun the simulations, which need rates and inflows.

The same paper builds larger circuits with the same recipe: an AND gate from two
NAND gates and an OR gate from three, where again one organization with the right
output remains for each input pair (except that their OR gate does not fix its
output from one input `b = 1` alone); an RS **flip-flop** from two cross-coupled
NAND gates, which has 25 organizations with no input and two or three for each
input pair, its memory showing up as two organizations, `{A, B, C, d}` and
`{A, B, c, D}`, for the same "hold" input; and a controllable **oscillator** from
a NAND gate fed back on itself. The oscillator only works after a catalytic
amplification step is added, and then shows up as a single organization that
contains both values of the oscillating bits. The authors note that the theory
says an oscillation is possible there but not more about it. Chemart generates
none of these circuits: only the XOR gate is implemented.

### The maximal independent set

Matsumaru and Dittrich (2006) applied the approach to the MIS program. On the
path of three vertices the network has **five organizations**: the empty set,
`{s0_1}`, `{s0_3}`, and the two answers `{s0_1, s1_2, s0_3}` ("010") and
`{s1_1, s0_2, s1_3}` ("101"). The small ones are "uncompleted computation due
to a lack of molecules", which enough starting molecules avoid. They point out
that these organizations do not form a lattice, since there is no single
largest one. On a triangle there are seven organizations, the three largest
being the three answers. On a six-vertex, seven-edge graph made of two
triangles joined by an edge (26 reactions), there are **49 organizations**, and
the **eight largest**, with six species each, are exactly the maximal
independent sets. A later poster (Matsumaru, Lenser, Hinze and Dittrich 2007)
states that this correspondence between the largest organizations and the
maximal independent sets can be proven for any graph.

Chemart reproduces these counts: the organization search finds the five
organizations of the three-vertex path, the seven of the triangle, and 49 organizations with eight of
size six on two triangles joined by an edge
(`graph=[[1,2],[2,3],[1,3],[4,5],[5,6],[4,6],[3,4]]`). The paper's figure does
not name the joining edge; by symmetry any choice gives the same graph. The test
`test_maximal_independent_set_rules` checks the three kinds of reaction on a
three-vertex path (one "join" reaction, both directions of the push-out
reaction, one annihilation).

### Robustness

The book reports, from Matsumaru, Lenser, Hinze and Dittrich's 2007 MIS paper,
that the answers are organizations and therefore robust: if `s0` or `s1`
molecules are added or removed, the system falls back into the MIS solution,
which is an attractor of the dynamics, and it should be able to reconfigure
itself when vertices are added or removed. This is the stated motivation for
the whole approach: organizations do not vanish. The 2006 paper proposes, but
does not run, a benchmark along these lines: sensor nodes in a line that must
settle into alternating states and repair themselves when a node is removed.
Chemart does not reproduce this: it has no rates and no simulator, and
robustness is a property of the dynamics, not of the reaction list. The 2007
paper itself was not available for this page, so its argument is not
summarised here.

### Later work

Matsumaru, Kreyssig and Dittrich (2011) review the approach and turn it into
design principles: one organization for each output class, the output inside
the closure of the input, unwanted organizations removed, no organization
below an output one (or stability guaranteed by the reactions alone), and
kinetics only for fine tuning. They set this constructive design beside
design by evolution and by exploration. Two evolutionary studies use the theory
as an analysis tool: Matsumaru et al. (2006) describe chemical evolution as
upward, downward and sideways movements between organizations, and Lenser et
al. (2008) track evolving chemical flip-flops and find, in the book's summary,
that evolutionary improvements mostly coincide with changes in organizational
structure. The book names one drawback: every state of every variable needs its
own species, since absence must be signalled by the presence of another
species, so these programs need even more species than computing with
concentrations.
